name: Mani Rimdu
when: Tengboche: October or November, set by the Tibetan lunar calendar; Thame: usually May; Chiwong in Solu also stages it
summary: Mani Rimdu is a 19-day ritual cycle at the Nyingma monasteries of Tengboche, Thame and Chiwong, ending in three public days of blessings, masked cham dances and a fire ceremony. For Khumbu Sherpas it is the biggest gathering of the year.
body: Mani Rimdu came to Khumbu from Rongbuk Monastery on the Tibetan side of Everest, where the lama Ngawang Tenzin Norbu began it in the early 1900s, drawing on the rituals of Mindroling, a great Nyingma monastery in central Tibet. Rongbuk's ties with Khumbu were close: it was Ngawang Tenzin Norbu who blessed Lama Gulu to found Tengboche in 1916. When Tibet's monasteries emptied after 1959, the Khumbu and Solu gompas became the keepers of the festival.

Most of the 19 days are private: monks build a sand mandala and chant to consecrate the mani rilbu, small blessed pills that give the festival its name. The public part comes at the end. On the first day lamas give the wang, a long-life empowerment, and hand the pills to the crowd. The second day is the dance day, when monks in brocade and painted masks perform the cham in the courtyard, acting out the defeat of forces hostile to the dharma, with comic interludes the Sherpa audience loves.

The final ceremony is a jinsek, a fire offering, followed by dances that dissolve the mandala's power back into the world. Families walk in from Namche, Khumjung, Pangboche and Phortse dressed in their best, and lodges in Tengboche fill. At Thame the festival usually falls in May; at Chiwong, on its cliff above Phaplu, it draws people from across Solu. Dates are fixed by the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Book Tengboche or Deboche rooms months ahead for the dance days, or sleep in Pangboche and walk over early
Sit where the monks show you, keep the dance floor clear, and never step over the ritual objects
Bring a down jacket: the courtyard dances run for hours in the cold shade of an autumn afternoon

faqs.q: When is Mani Rimdu at Tengboche?
faqs.a: Tengboche's Mani Rimdu falls in October or November, set by the Tibetan lunar calendar, so the Western dates change every year. The public days, the blessing, the masked dances and the fire ceremony, come at the end of the 19-day cycle and usually land near a full moon. Thame holds its own Mani Rimdu, usually in May. Check current status before you travel.

Yes. The three public days are open to anyone, and many trekkers time their Everest walk to pass Tengboche then. There is no ticket, though a donation to the monastery is welcome. Photography of the dances is generally allowed from the edges; inside the prayer hall, ask first. Dress warmly, arrive early for a place on the steps, and stay for the whole sequence rather than a single dance.

The name comes from mani rilbu, the small blessed pills consecrated during the festival's secret rituals and handed out on the empowerment day. Mani refers to the mantra of compassion, om mani padme hum, which monks chant thousands of times over the pills. Receiving them is considered a blessing for long life, and Sherpa families keep them at home.

Three: Tengboche in Khumbu, the best known and most visited; Thame, west of Namche on the old trade route to Tibet; and Chiwong in Solu, on a cliff above Phaplu. All three trace the ritual to Rongbuk Monastery in Tibet. Thame's is usually in May, Tengboche's in October or November. Check current status before you travel, as dates follow the lunar calendar.

name: Dumji
when: Usually June or July, in the fifth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar
summary: Dumji is a Sherpa village festival that marks the birth of Guru Rinpoche, held in Namche and other Khumbu and Solu villages in the early monsoon. Sponsoring households feed the whole village for several days of rituals, masked dances and feasting.
body: Where Mani Rimdu belongs to the monasteries, Dumji belongs to the village. It honours the birth of Guru Rinpoche, Padmasambhava, the teacher who in Sherpa belief brought Buddhism over the Himalaya and blessed Khumbu as a hidden, sacred valley. It falls in the fifth Tibetan month, usually June or July, when the potatoes are in and the trekking season has ended, so it is a festival held by Sherpas for Sherpas.

The heart of Dumji is obligation. Each year a few households take their turn as sponsors, and for them it is a large expense: they provide food and chhang for everyone over several days, and the honour is real. Village lamas, many of them married householders rather than celibate monks, perform rituals in the village gompa, followed by masked dances. In Namche the dances take place in the courtyard of the village gompa.

For travellers, Dumji is a monsoon event. Flights to Lukla are unreliable in June and July, trails below Namche are wet and leech-prone, and clouds hide the peaks. Those who come anyway see Khumbu without the crowds, at home with itself. Dates differ from village to village and are set locally, so check current status before you travel and ask your guide to confirm which village is celebrating.
tips: Allow two or three spare days in Kathmandu either side, because monsoon flights to Lukla are often cancelled
Carry a small gift or donation for the sponsoring household if you are invited to eat
Ask before photographing ritual dances inside the gompa; outside, keep a respectful distance

faqs.q: When is Dumji celebrated in Namche Bazaar?
faqs.a: Dumji usually falls in June or July, in the fifth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, marking the birth of Guru Rinpoche. Each village sets its own dates, so Namche's may not match those of neighbouring villages. Because it lands in the monsoon, flights and weather are unreliable. Check current status before you travel and build in spare days.

faqs.q: Is Dumji worth planning a trip around?
faqs.a: For travellers interested in Sherpa village life, yes, with the right expectations. You will see a community festival, not a show: rituals, dances and long communal meals funded by sponsoring families. The trade-off is monsoon weather, cloudy peaks and flight delays. We suggest it for repeat visitors who already know Khumbu and want to see it at home, not for a first Everest trek.

Over several days, village lamas perform rituals in the gompa, masked dances follow, and the sponsoring households serve food and chhang to the whole community. The sponsoring households rotate each year, and hosting is both a heavy expense and a real honour. It is as much about feeding neighbours and settling community bonds as about ritual.

Dumji is held in several Sherpa villages of Khumbu and Solu, Namche among them, each with its own village gompa and dates. Your guide's family network is the best way to find out which village is celebrating during your stay. Because it is a local event rather than a tourist one, dates are rarely published far ahead. Check current status before you travel.

name: Gyalpo Lhosar (Sherpa New Year)
when: February or March, the first day of the Tibetan lunar year
summary: Gyalpo Lhosar is the Tibetan lunar new year that Sherpa families in Khumbu and Solu celebrate in February or March, with house cleaning, new prayer flags, monastery visits and days of visiting relatives. It is a national public holiday in Nepal.
body: Lhosar means new year, and Gyalpo, king, refers to the royal new year of the Tibetan calendar that Sherpas share with Tibetans and other Himalayan Buddhists. Nepal marks it as a public holiday. In Khumbu it arrives at the cold, quiet end of winter, when many lodges are shut and families who spent the season in Kathmandu often come home.

The days before are for cleaning. Houses are swept, the old year's bad luck is thrown out, and new prayer flags go up on rooftops and passes. On the day itself families visit the gompa, offer white khata scarves and butter lamps, and then go from house to house. Every host pours chhang or tea and expects you to accept at least three times. Food is rich for winter: fried khapse biscuits, meat, and plenty of butter tea.

For visitors, Lhosar is a good reason to walk in late February or early March. Nights are well below freezing above Namche and some high lodges are still closed, but the trails are empty, the light is sharp and the villages are at their most hospitable. Dates follow the lunar calendar and shift each year; check current status before you travel.
tips: Accept chhang or tea with your right hand, or both hands, and sip rather than refuse outright
Carry a white khata scarf if you plan to visit a gompa or a family; shops in Namche sell them
Walk with warm layers: February nights in Khumjung often fall below minus 10 °C

faqs.a: Sherpas celebrate Gyalpo Lhosar, the Tibetan lunar new year, which usually falls in February or early March. The exact date changes every year with the lunar calendar. Nepal's government declares it a public holiday, so offices and some shops close. In Khumbu, celebrations run for several days of gompa visits and family calls. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it a good time to trek to Everest during Lhosar?
faqs.a: It can be, if you handle cold well. Trails are quiet, skies often clear and villages are festive. The catch is temperature: nights in Khumjung and Namche drop well below freezing, and above Dingboche many lodges stay closed until March. We suggest lower routes such as Namche, Khumjung and Tengboche at Lhosar rather than a full Base Camp trek.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Sherpa Lhosar and Tamang Lhosar?
faqs.a: Nepal has three Lhosars. Tamang communities celebrate Sonam Lhosar in January or February, Gurungs mark Tamu Lhosar at the end of December, and Sherpas, along with Tibetans, celebrate Gyalpo Lhosar in February or March. All three are new year festivals, but they follow different calendars and traditions, and each is a public holiday in Nepal.

faqs.q: How should visitors behave at a Lhosar celebration?
faqs.a: Accept what is offered, at least a sip, with your right hand or both hands, and say tashi delek, the Sherpa and Tibetan greeting for good fortune. Walk clockwise around chortens and inside gompas. Ask before taking photos of people or altars. A small gift such as fruit or biscuits is welcome if a family invites you in.
